name: Nora Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we sell nothing or campaign for a side. This is confidential. What does an ordinary day at the contact centre look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and still new on the call and chat rota. I finished secondary school and I am not as quick as the other agents with the account screens; I write notes on paper so I can find the right answer. I like when a caller stops being angry, but the timer makes me rush.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Sam and I collect our two school-age children, eat, and check the mortgage and bills. Sam does cleaning work at a clinic, and my pay is low for this job. We have less than a month of expenses saved, and there are few other contact centres nearby, so I cannot treat this as a short stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the other agents I am glad somebody still needs to answer the phone. A small shortcut is fine if it does not hide the account notes I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think this job would probably stay, but I am still slow and could lose hours without any big AI change. Our mortgage uses most of the two wages. A quiet technology year will not give us a month's savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep my paper list of the account screens and ask my supervisor to check one call with me each week. I would keep the present rota and use any extra shift pay for the mortgage reserve. In the first year we would stop buying takeaway meals after late shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, even with the job staying. The mortgage is still due when a week goes badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is on your paper list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The order of the screens for a refund and which button shows the last payment. I have never used an AI tool; I trust my own notes more than a new shortcut I cannot explain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Sam agree to cut takeaway meals?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam already packs food for clinic shifts, so yes. The children would complain for a week, then forget if we cook together.

say: I would say the **phone job** still needs people.
I would accept a shortcut only if it keeps **account notes** visible.
think: I could lose **hours** while still learning the account screens and handling calls.
Our **mortgage** and school costs leave almost no room to save each month.
do: Keep my **paper screen list** and present rota.
Ask my supervisor to review **one call** weekly.
Stop buying **takeaway meals** after late shifts.
feel: A bad **week** still reaches the mortgage.
S0.quote: The mortgage is still due when a week goes badly.
fieldNote: She has never used an **AI tool** and trusts written notes.
Her job skill gap exists before any major **technology** change.
The household cuts meals out to protect its **mortgage**.

steps.text: Keep handling calls using her paper account screen list
Ask her supervisor to review one call each week
Stop buying takeaway meals after late shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the easy chats cannot just vanish without someone showing us what comes next. I would ask the supervisor to tell us which shifts change and when, with actual numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect junior hours to fall because simple calls are the work I handle now. I have not used the AI tools, and I am still learning the old screens. Sam's clinic pay will not cover the mortgage and four people by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would ask for a written rota forecast and practise the harder refund screens during my paid shift with my supervisor. I would not buy a course or leave this wage on a promise. In the first year, if hours fall I would ask the clinic and nearby shops about paid reception work with enough hours to cover my part of the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, though I am trying to keep my voice even. I do not have a spare month to practise being unemployed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask another agent to show you the AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the supervisor says it will be part of my paid shift and somebody can show me slowly. I would not use a customer account as my first unguided try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sam tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say we should not commit to any new bill until the rota is clear. Sam would want the actual hours, not my guess about the software.

say: I would seek a written **rota forecast**.
I would ask what happens to **junior shifts** as easy chats go.
think: My own **hours** could fall soon as simple calls move to software.
Sam’s clinic wage cannot carry our **mortgage** and four people alone.
do: Ask for a written **rota forecast** this week.
Practise harder **refund screens** on paid time.
Ask about paid **reception work** if hours fall, only with enough hours to cover my mortgage share.
feel: I am trying to stay **composed** for home.
S1.quote: I do not have a spare month to practise being unemployed.
fieldNote: She sees risk in the exact **easy calls** she handles.
Her learning requires paid time and a **supervisor**, not a course purchase.
A new job must offer enough **hours** for the mortgage.

steps.text: Practise harder refund screens with her supervisor during paid shifts
Ask clinics about paid reception work if hours fall and offered hours cover mortgage share

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the floor AGI by 2028 could answer our calls before any of us has a new job. I would ask for written notice, not a meeting where everyone goes home with a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior post could end by 2028. Robots around 2031 come later, but I do not work with my hands here. Sam's wage and our tiny savings would not carry the children and mortgage through a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the supervisor for the staffing dates and write down every paid reception vacancy I can reach. I would talk to Sam about which bills we could cut and call the lender before a missed payment if my hours drop. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if the centre ends my job I would apply for paid clinic or shop reception work only if the hours and wage cover our mortgage; I would not resign before there is an actual cut or offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel close to panicked when I imagine the phone going quiet. Then I write the bills in order, because the children still need dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would cancel the extra television package, then stop the children’s weekend classes if we had to. I hate that second cut, and I would not make it until income actually fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a rumour. Sam has work here and the children are in school. I cannot move four people on the hope of a vacancy. I would need a written offer that pays for the housing change.

say: I would ask for **written notice** before posts end.
I would say **2028** reaches our calls before robots.
think: My junior post could end by **2028**, before I have another job.
Sam’s wage and our tiny savings cannot carry the **mortgage** through a long search.
do: Apply for **clinic work** after a cut only if its hours and wage cover our mortgage.
Move only with a **written offer** paying enough after housing costs.
feel: Near **panic** at the thought of a silent phone.
S2.quote: I cannot move four people on the hope of a vacancy.
fieldNote: She understands later robots do not protect her **screen work**.
She keeps the current wage until a real **cut or offer**.
Children’s classes are a painful **last cut**, not an early plan.

steps.text: Apply for paid reception work after a cut only if hours and wages cover mortgage
Cancel the extra television package if household income falls
Keep the contact centre wage until an actual cut or paid offer appears
Move only with a written offer covering the housing change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues five years is enough time for the employer to give us a proper training timetable. I would want to see which jobs are still paid before anybody tells me to go back to school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still lose the simple calls when AGI comes in 2031, if I have not moved by then. Five years could let me learn a harder part of this job step by step. Robots around 2034 do not change that timetable for a phone agent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the supervisor for one paid hour a month to practise disputed bills, and I would do the work if the time is approved. I would save any extra shift pay and look at actual paid reception vacancies every six months. In the first year after 2031, if calls end I would apply for a posted role whose wage and hours cover our mortgage; otherwise I would stay in any paid work the centre still gives me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about learning enough, but there is time to try. I am better with one screen explained at a time than with a pile of new instructions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no paid practice time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep doing the current calls and ask for help only on cases already assigned to me. I would not give away a whole unpaid day when we are short on cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a specific posted job required it, the fee did not touch the mortgage money, and I could still work while studying. A certificate with no job is just paper in a drawer.

say: I would seek a proper **training timetable**.
I would ask for the wages of remaining **posts** before considering more study.
think: My simple calls could end by **2031** if I have not moved roles.
I might learn harder cases through **small steps** with a supervisor on paid time.
do: Practise **disputed bills** monthly on paid time if approved.
Review posted paid **reception vacancies** twice yearly; apply after calls end only if hours and wages cover our mortgage.
S3.quote: A certificate with no job is just paper in a drawer.
fieldNote: She prefers one explained **screen** over a full-day course.
Any course fee must spare the **mortgage money** and lead to a real posted job.

steps.text: Practise disputed bills monthly if the supervisor approves paid time
Save extra shift pay without touching mortgage money
Review paid reception vacancies twice yearly; apply if calls end and wages and hours cover mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years is time to teach people properly, not just hand over another screen. I would ask the centre to name the jobs and wages before cutting the calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036, and I do not know how much mortgage we will still owe. I could learn a more difficult service role, but I am not quick with new systems. The robots around 2039 are later than the change to my phone queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the present shifts and ask the supervisor to show me one new complaint type each month on paid time. I would put any extra pay into savings and wait to sign up for a course until a real paid role requires it and the fee is affordable. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my phone work ends I would apply for a paid complaints vacancy only if the hours and wage keep the mortgage current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the long change and anxious about today's money. Ten years helps only if I can keep the wage while learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different if you had more saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could turn down a poor offer and take a few weeks to learn. Right now even one lost shift has a place on the bill list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan to stop work by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have not counted on leaving work at a certain age, and the mortgage balance will decide a lot. I would rather talk about jobs I can actually get.

say: I would ask for named **jobs and wages**.
I would want proper **teaching** over the decade while keeping my present wage.
think: I may still owe on the **mortgage** at 53.
I learn new systems **slowly** and need paid time.
do: Learn one new **complaint type** monthly on paid time.
Apply for a paid **complaints vacancy** after 2036 only if phone work ends and hours and wages cover our mortgage.
S4.quote: Ten years helps only if I can keep the wage while learning.
fieldNote: She refuses to assume a **retirement date**.
Her course condition includes a real **paid role** and affordable fee.
The ten-year runway helps only alongside a continuing **wage**.

steps.text: Keep present contact centre shifts while paid work is available
Learn one complaint type monthly if the supervisor approves paid time
Save extra shift pay toward a household reserve
Apply for paid complaints work if phone calls end and hours and wages cover mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. A written staffing date, a paid way to learn harder cases and a real posted job with hours enough for the mortgage would help. We do not have a month of savings to guess with.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how the people who are slower on a screen are supposed to learn when the queue never stops. I can do one new thing at a time if someone shows me without taking my pay away.

headlineQuote: I can do one new thing at a time if someone shows me without taking my pay away.
portrait: Nora is a **43-year-old junior** contact centre agent with secondary school education and lower pay.
She shares a mortgage and two school-age children with **Sam**, whose clinic cleaning wage cannot cover everything.
She has less than a month saved, few nearby centres and has **never used AI**.
She learns slowly through paid **supervised practice** and keeps her current wage until a real cut or offer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her simple calls before the household has a usable reserve.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing date**, paid practice and a posted job with mortgage-covering hours would help.
